newsitem.title: UK: New British P.M. arrivs in troubled N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: New British P.M. arrivs in troubled N.Ireland.

text.p: Britain's new Prime Minister Tony Blair arrived in troubled Northern Ireland on Friday to underline his Labour government's commitment to seek an end to 28 years of sectarian and political conflict.
Blair's one-day visit, his first outside London since he came to power in May 1 elections, took place against a backdrop of continued violence which has killed three people in 10 days.
The Prime Minister was expected to pledge continued efforts to try to forge a political settlement through multi-party talks which resume in Belfast on June 3 after months of deadlock.
His first stop was the southern border city of Armagh. The rest of his itinerary was not published for security reasons.
Officials said Blair would be receiving a security briefing in Armagh from police and army chiefs on the conlict, in which 3,200 people have been killed over the past quarter century.

No new initiatives were expected from Blair but his visit was seen as signifying that his administration would attach a high priority to solving one of Britain's longest and costliest problems and one of Europe's oldest guerrilla wars.

The Labour party and the Conservative government it routed on May 1 adopted a bi-partisan approach to Northern Ireland aimed at getting Unionists, who want the province to stay British, and Irish nationalists to agree a lasting solution.
The negotiations exclude the Irish Republican Army's political wing Sinn Fein because of a decision by the guerrillas to resume their war against British rule last year after a 17-month ceasefire.

David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, the province's biggest pro-British grouping, said he welcomed Blair's commitment in a parliamentary speech to ban Sinn Fein until there was a genuine IRA ceasefire.

"I must approve of the language that Tony Blair used in the Commons in his first speech as Prime Minister when he said that Sinn Fein/IRA have to decisively turn away from violence and commit themselves to the peace process once and for all.
"I think that's right. We needn't look at fancy formulae. It's a question of is there a genuine commitment to peace and democracy which is made once and for all?" he told BBC radio.
Blair was expected to reassert that there would be no place for Sinn Fein at the Belfast talks until the IRA declared a new, credible ceasefire signalling a complete halt to their war.

Sinn Fein leaders Gerry Adams and Martin McGuinness were both elected to the British parliament in the May 1 election but have refused to occupy their seats because it would entail an oath of allegiance to the British rule they want to end.
They say they should be at the Belfast talks by virtue of their electoral mandate, but Britain says no party can take part while it has armed backers ready to contest any settlement.

Daily violence in Northern Ireland has ebbed considerably since the IRA's original 1994 ceasefire. In the early 1990s some 80 people a year were killed either by Irish republicans or so-called Loyalists fighting to maintain British rule.

The conflict is an enormous drain on British government coffers, which provide some four billion sterling ($6 billion) a year to pay for a vast security operation involving thousands of troops and police.
The conflict has exploded sporadically both in Britain and Northern Ireland, triggering a wave of attacks by Loyalists in recent weeks in apparent retaliation for IRA actions.
Two Roman Catholics have died violently in the past week after the Irish National Liberation Army (INLA), a shadowy IRA offshoot, shot an off-duty policeman in a bar.
